desc:
A chocolate bar consists of consecutive chunks, chunk i having sweetness sweetness[i]. You want to share it with k friends, so you cut the bar into exactly k + 1 pieces, each made of one or more consecutive chunks. You are polite and keep the piece with the least total sweetness for yourself, giving the sweeter pieces to your friends.

Return the largest total sweetness your own piece can have if you cut optimally.

Example: sweetness = [1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2], k = 2. Cut into [1,2,2,1,2], [2,1,2], [2]... that leaves a piece of 2, which is poor; the better cut [1,2,2], [1,2,2], [1,2,2] gives every piece 5. The answer is 5.
hints: You want the minimum piece to be large. What is a simple question you can ask about a target value x?
Can the bar be cut into at least k + 1 pieces that each have total sweetness at least x? Cut greedily: close a piece as soon as it reaches x.

If target x is achievable, so is every smaller target (sweetness is positive). Binary search x from min(sweetness) to sum // (k + 1), looking for the largest achievable one. Leftover chunks at the end can simply be merged into the last piece.
editorial: Fix a target x and ask whether we can form at least k + 1 pieces each of sum at least x. Scan left to right, adding chunks to the current piece and closing it as soon as its sum reaches x. Closing as early as possible leaves the most chunks for later pieces, so this greedy produces the maximum number of pieces. Any leftover chunks at the end are glued onto the last piece, which only makes it sweeter, so having at least k + 1 closed pieces is enough (extra pieces are merged into neighbours).

The check is monotone in x: a larger target is harder. The answer lies between min(sweetness) (each chunk alone, when there are enough chunks, or lower targets) and sum // (k + 1) (the average piece). We binary search for the largest feasible x in O(n log sum) time and O(1) space. This is the mirror image of the classic 'minimise the largest piece' split problem.
